name: ClickHouse
blurb: Tinybird · ChistaData · Altinity · official — operating, MVs, schema, Keeper, war stories

sections.name: Operating the cluster — the runbook canon

entries.title: I've operated petabyte-scale ClickHouse clusters for 5 years (Part I)
entries.body: The architecture bible. Don't shard prematurely ("re-sharding was super hard"). ZK on isolated machines. Capacity rule: 32 cores ≈ 5GB/s. Wait a month after any release. Batch inserts, aim for one part per insert.

entries.title: Lessons learned from 5 years with ClickHouse clusters: Part II
entries.body: The monitoring + DDL runbook. ON CLUSTER stalls when a replica is down. "Read only tables → you are fucked" recovery: drop, recreate, let replication refill. The POPULATE-is-broken warning and the uniqExactState-kills-merges warning both originate here.

entries.title: Hunting orphan objects: 45% off our storage bill (and a near data-loss incident)
entries.body: A cleanup job that continued on incomplete snapshots classified live objects as dead → "file not found" at query time. Two paths on disk: runtime uses store/\<uuid>/, backups use data/\<db>/\<table>/. Pre-stage the UUID↔table map before you need it.

entries.title: How we handle service disruptions
entries.body: 28-min outage from config drift — one environment had a different data path. Two lessons: LB health checks must verify data returned, not just liveness; and staging-passes ≠ prod-safe when config has drifted.

entries.title: Why we maintain a ClickHouse fork at Tinybird
entries.body: Doubles as an upgrade-pain field report. "Pretty much any time you upgrade you have some issues." Documents the UNION + MV silent-drop regression in 25.8.1.477. The case for a query-replay validation harness before every upgrade. Zero-copy disabled by default ≥ v22.8.

entries.title: We added the Backup Database engine to ClickHouse
entries.body: Backup Database engine ships in 25.2. Attach a backup as a read-only DB in seconds — no full restore. The cheapest way to run production-data upgrade validation without a parallel cluster.

entries.title: Resolving a year-long ClickHouse lock contention
entries.body: CPU at 20% but QPS capped → contention, not resources. They added ContextLockWaitMicroseconds (PR #55029) to make it visible, then refactored Context. Result: 3× QPS at concurrency 500, 5×+ at 1000. Put this profile event on your dashboards day one.

entries.title: ClickHouse Grafana mix-in (dashboard + alert rules)
entries.body: The source of truth for exact metric names. The dashboard JSON shows CPU as CGroupUserTimeNormalized × 100. Anything not in here, validate before alerting on it.

entries.title: system.asynchronous\_metrics (replication signals)
entries.body: Source of the highest-priority alerts: ReadonlyReplica > 0 (page now), ReplicasMaxAbsoluteDelay, ReplicasMaxQueueSize, MaxPartCountForPartition (TOO\_MANY\_PARTS proximity — default throw at 300).

entries.title: ClickHouse Keeper — monitoring & 4LW commands
entries.body: Keeper Raft state lives behind the mntr four-letter-word on port 9181 (zk\_followers, zk\_synced\_followers) — not on the Prometheus endpoint. ClickHouseMetrics\_KeeperAliveConnections reads 0 in some versions (issue #60742); validate before relying.

entries.title: How to optimize a ClickHouse cluster
entries.body: The slow-query hunt against system.query\_log (query\_duration\_ms > 1000). Recommends background\_pool\_size ≈ 20–30% of cores; flags parts\_to\_throw\_insert=600 as a streaming-tuned value vs OSS 300.

entries.title: How we processed 12 trillion rows during Black Friday
entries.body: 35M rows/sec read average. The operational nugget: system tables eat disk under load. Set TTLs on system.query\_log, part\_log, metric\_log; disable query\_thread\_log if unused.

entries.title: Access Rights & Account Management
entries.body: The bootstrap dance (access\_management=1, lock down default). The ALTER hierarchy trap: ALTER ROW POLICY/USER/QUOTA are not children of ALTER — grant explicitly. Privileges survive table drops.

entries.title: CREATE QUOTA
entries.body: The runaway-dashboard defense: KEYED BY normalized\_query\_hash. Quota counters live on the receiving node — on a 9×2 behind an LB, effective limit = N × quota unless you pin sessions. Quotas reset on restart.

entries.title: CREATE USER
entries.body: Prefer bcrypt\_password. Production hosts: HOST IP only (host\_regexp adds latency). The VALID UNTIL timezone trap — no IANA names, compute the offset (e.g. +03:00).

entries.title: CREATE ROW POLICY
entries.body: Defining any policy on a table hides it from all non-mentioned users — pair with a TO ALL EXCEPT allow-policy. Multi-tenant pattern: USING tenant\_id = getSetting('SQL\_tenant\_id'). Only safe for readonly users.

entries.title: HTTP Authenticator (the Keycloak bridge)
entries.body: Basic scheme + GET only — no Bearer. But the auth server's JSON response can return a settings object that becomes session settings → return SQL\_tenant\_id from a Keycloak introspection proxy and drive row policies off it.

entries.title: External Authenticators (LDAP / Kerberos / SSL / HTTP)
entries.body: The complete self-managed list — no OIDC/JWT on OSS server (Cloud only). For Keycloak: LDAP federation (no claims), HTTP-proxy introspection (claims via settings), a fronting proxy like chproxy, or SSL certs from Keycloak's CA.

sections.name: Materialized views — insert triggers, not snapshots

entries.title: CREATE VIEW — all view types
entries.body: The "implemented like insert triggers" definition. Normal / Materialized / Refreshable / Window. Default security is DEFINER (not INVOKER) — MVs bypass the inserting user's row policies.

entries.title: Incremental Materialized View guide
entries.body: The AggregatingMergeTree + -State / -Merge workhorse pattern. Non-negotiable rule: destination ORDER BY must equal the MV GROUP BY, else merges leave duplicate rows.

entries.title: Refreshable Materialized View
entries.body: Scheduled, atomic-swap, no restrictions on the SELECT (UNION, JOIN, table functions all work) — the answer to the JOIN trap. Status in system.view\_refreshes. DEPENDS ON chains. Experimental 23.12 → production-ready 24.10.

entries.title: Materialized views — community wisdom (the 190 GB explosion)
entries.body: A 20GB table exploded to 190GB via an MV (one row per attribute). The aggregation-ratio query: if uniq(group\_by)/count() > 70%, don't build the MV. Run it on every proposal.

entries.title: How to fix Kafka → ClickHouse performance bottlenecks
entries.body: The customer with three cascading MVs creating a chain reaction on every append. The direct argument for capping MV chain depth at 2 on high-volume ingest paths.

entries.title: Best practices to backfill materialized views
entries.body: The silent-partial-failure trap: a backfill that dies mid-way leaves undetectable incomplete data. Recipe: stage per chunk, validate, atomically rename/move. An 8-day backfill cut down via parallel on-demand replicas.

entries.title: Performance impact of materialized views
entries.body: The hard numbers: \~55% throughput loss at 1 MV, \~90% at 10 (100-row batches). Batch size dominates MV cost — the strongest argument for a Null-engine landing buffer.

entries.title: ClickHouse MVs: How they work and where they break
entries.body: Block-level mechanics (max\_insert\_block\_size = 1,048,576), the JOIN trap, why TO tables beat implicit .inner. tables. The clearest single explainer corroborating the docs.

entries.title: PostHog ClickHouse data-ingestion handbook
entries.body: The Kafka-engine → \_mv → sharded-events pattern. The DETACH limbo trap: a non-PERMANENTLY detach re-attaches on restart. Schema-as-code via their open-source chschema.

entries.title: MVs as alternative primary indexes
entries.body: One table = one primary index. An MV maintains a second sort order for the opposite access pattern: main table by time, MV by trace\_id for point lookups. Directly relevant to the lookup-vs-rollup tension on event tables.

entries.title: Using Materialized Views in ClickHouse
entries.body: The official conceptual intro — engines, combinators, the read-side -Merge story. Good for onboarding teammates before they touch the production MV DDL.

sections.name: ReplacingMergeTree — dedup at merge, not insert

entries.title: ReplacingMergeTree engine reference
entries.body: "Eventual correctness only — don't rely on it." Highest version wins; is\_deleted only filters under FINAL. OPTIMIZE FINAL CLEANUP needs the experimental flag. Deletes recommended only for \<10% delete rate.

entries.title: Working with ReplacingMergeTree (operator guide)
entries.body: do\_not\_merge\_across\_partitions\_select\_final=1 parallelizes FINAL per partition. The merge-stops-trap: parts past max\_bytes\_to\_merge\_at\_max\_space\_in\_pool never auto-merge again — schedule OPTIMIZE on cold partitions.

entries.title: ReplacingMergeTree — The Good, The Bad, The Ugly
entries.body: The honest tradeoff write-up. Why clean\_deleted\_rows='Always' had correctness issues on replicated tables (issue #50346) — prefer scheduled OPTIMIZE FINAL CLEANUP until verified for your version.

entries.title: SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA after metadata loss
entries.body: Bulk corrections via insert-higher-version (not ALTER UPDATE). When metadata is lost a replica attaches read-only; SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA … ON CLUSTER rebuilds it without deleting data.

entries.title: Manipulating Partitions and Parts
entries.body: REPLACE PARTITION is atomic; plain ATTACH PARTITION FROM is hardlink-based but not labelled atomic. Same-disk + same storage-policy required or it falls back to a real copy.

entries.title: How we built branches: sharing production data without copying it
entries.body: Zero-copy partition sharing via cloneAndLoadDataPart() — hardlinks on the same disk, reference counts on S3. Parts are immutable, which is the whole reason ATTACH is cheap and safe.

entries.title: ClickHouse schema migrations 2026 (EXCHANGE TABLES)
entries.body: EXCHANGE TABLES a AND b swaps names atomically — queries never see an intermediate state. The safe whole-table swap for schema changes that ATTACH PARTITION can't handle (changed ORDER BY / partition key / column types).

entries.title: Altinity KB — schema migration tools index
entries.body: The curated link-list: golang-migrate (their pick), Flyway (community), Bytebase, dbmate, Alembic, plus Python/PHP tools. By giving golang-migrate the only detail page, it's the de-facto recommendation.

entries.title: golang-migrate for ClickHouse
entries.body: Single binary, no JRE. State in schema\_migrations. Cluster replication via x-cluster-name. Clustered support since v4.15.0.

entries.title: golang-migrate ClickHouse driver (README)
entries.body: Default TinyLog engine for the state table breaks clickhouse-backup — set x-migrations-table-engine=MergeTree. No multi-statement per file unless x-multi-statement (naive; split, non-transactional). The dirty=1 lock needs manual recovery.

entries.title: ClickHouse KB — schema migration tools
entries.body: The official categorization: write-SQL-run-in-CI (Goose, golang-migrate) vs governance platforms (Bytebase, Liquibase) vs declarative (Atlas). Confirms Atlas cluster support landed v0.37 (Sep 2025).

entries.title: Flyway ClickHouse driver reference
entries.body: Community-tier, separate flyway-database-clickhouse JAR (10.24.0, Aug 2025). First-class Cluster Name + Zookeeper Path config. Stalled-PRs history is the yellow flag — only if you already run Flyway elsewhere.

entries.title: Replication problems & DDL queue (runbook)
entries.body: Read-only tables → DROP / RESTORE REPLICA (recreates ZK metadata, deletes no data). Check system.replicas cluster-wide first. Watch num\_tries > 100 in the replication queue.

entries.title: DDL completes but stays stuck in distributed\_ddl\_queue
entries.body: A TRUNCATE … ON CLUSTER succeeded everywhere but stayed 'Active' in the queue past distributed\_ddl\_task\_timeout (180s). The "they will execute in background" message — the DDL didn't fail, it timed out.

entries.title: Stuck DDL worker on replica down
entries.body: One stuck task blocks all subsequent DDL because the worker is single-threaded on the queue. The cascade you most want to avoid — alert on queue age.

entries.title: DDLWorker fails ON CLUSTER — regression in v25.8.10.7-lts
entries.body: All ON CLUSTER DDLs fail on first install: "There is no a local address in host list." Carried forward across LTS tags. Proof the LTS label doesn't catch every regression — replay-harness before upgrade.

entries.title: Keeper causing replicas to turn read-only
entries.body: A team built an identical cluster on Keeper (vs ZooKeeper); random replicas went read-only for days, merges restarted from scratch. They migrated back to ZooKeeper to fix it. Worth knowing the failure shape exists.

entries.title: No maintenance mode when Keeper quorum is lost
entries.body: Open feature request: there's no way to access data or reconfigure when quorum is gone — recovery mode or nothing. Sets expectations for your worst-case Keeper DR rehearsal.

entries.title: How to handle a ClickHouse Keeper quorum loss
entries.body: The 4LW triage sequence: echo ruok \| nc host 9181, echo isro for read-only state, look for Mode: leader. A practical recovery walkthrough to adapt into your runbook.

sections.name: Customer war stories — MVs & scale at the edge

entries.title: HTTP analytics for 6M requests/sec using ClickHouse
entries.body: The canonical reference: 8 ReplicatedAggregatingMergeTree MVs off one raw table, each a different breakdown, queried in parallel for dashboards. 36-node cluster, 3× replication.

entries.title: How we make sense of too much data (downsampling)
entries.body: 700M+ events/sec, scan 96 trillion events in an hour, sub-2s. The 2018 MV architecture held — they evolved by adding downsampling, not rearchitecting MVs away.

entries.title: PostHog ClickHouse operations handbook
entries.body: 33 MVs + 38 ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree tables managed as code. Orphan ZK records pre-22.3, the kafka\_ingestion\_warnings pattern for broken messages. Honest operational detail from a heavy user.

entries.title: Lovable: refreshable MVs for periodic checks
entries.body: The clean split: incremental MVs for dashboards, refreshable MVs re-checked hourly for alerting. Four tables + four MVs powering the whole thing.

entries.title: Superwall: MVs were "like magic"
entries.body: 100 MB/sec ingest, 300 TB, +40 TB/month. Leaned on MVs instead of custom counter-update jobs. Cites Cloudflare + PostHog blogs as the confidence proof — the same lineage you're reading.

entries.title: Laravel Nightwatch: 1M events/sec observability
entries.body: MSK → ClickHouse at 1M events/sec sustained. MVs pre-aggregate raw JSON into query-ready form; time-series partitioning + codecs keep queries sub-second. A close analogue to a Flink → ClickHouse ingest shape.

entries.title: Cloudflare: scaling to quadrillions of rows
entries.body: The long-view companion — how the architecture compounded over years. Useful evidence for the "this scales" argument.

entries.title: Operator issue #750 — Data rebalancing not supported
entries.body: ClickHouse can't rebalance data; reducing shard count in YAML loses it. If you'll scale 9×2→12×2 later, build the rebalancing pipeline now — there is no 'just change the count' path.

entries.title: KB — Distributed table to a new cluster (MV-based shift)
entries.body: No-downtime resharding: stand up the new-shape cluster, mirror inserts via a Distributed MV, cut over, then backfill history separately. Cleaner than clickhouse-copier for incremental moves.

entries.title: The Curse of Regional Traffic
entries.body: Cross-AD rebalancing/backfill is billed on both ingress and egress at most clouds; co-locate or throttle the backfill, and prefer Native/Parquet over JSON-over-HTTP.

entries.title: ClickHouse Data Distribution
entries.body: Sharding and replication are orthogonal and baked in at CREATE TABLE — define tables Replicated from day one (you also get ZK-tracked dedup of the last 100 insert blocks).

entries.title: KB — Settings to adjust (production discipline list)
entries.body: Settings most likely to bite a 9×2: insert\_distributed\_sync, fsync\_\*, insert\_quorum, do\_not\_merge\_across\_partitions\_select\_final, inactive\_parts\_to\_throw\_insert.

entries.title: KB — Network configuration for cluster nodes
entries.body: Firewall ports (9000 native, 9009 interserver, 2181/9181 Keeper), 10 Gbit between nodes, AD separation for replicas, and keep inter-replica round-trip under \~20 ms.

entries.title: KB — Using clickhouse-keeper (migration mechanics)
entries.body: A mixed ZK/Keeper quorum is unsupported and snapshot formats differ; convert from a stopped ZK leader, or start empty and rebuild metadata via SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA per table.

entries.title: KB — ZooKeeper backup (TL;DR: don't)
entries.body: Don't back up ZK/Keeper — a snapshot is incoherent with on-disk data. Back up ClickHouse data and rebuild Keeper's view with SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA. Inverts the usual operator instinct.

entries.title: KB — ZooKeeper care & feeding
entries.body: Hard rules: NVMe for the txn log, 3 nodes (not 5), never co-locate with ClickHouse, set autopurge. 'Slow ZooKeeper' is usually a ClickHouse-side symptom (too many parts/tables).

entries.title: What's new in the Altinity Kubernetes Operator
entries.body: Its CHK Keeper-replacement runbook is the cleanest end-to-end one published — including that mount paths must match or the new Keeper won't find its state. Useful even on bare metal.

entries.title: CVEs, ClickHouse, and Altinity.Cloud
entries.body: The access\_control\_improvements block (off by default): row-policy default-deny, ON CLUSTER requires grant, table\_engines\_require\_grant, plus remote\_url\_allow\_hosts to close SSRF via url()/s3().

entries.title: Integrating ClickHouse with LDAP, Part 1
entries.body: LDAP for auth of local users, or as an external user directory mapping LDAP groups to ClickHouse roles — the latter eliminates per-user CREATE USER entirely.

entries.title: OAuth in Altinity Builds
entries.body: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC support landing in Altinity Stable — token-based, Keycloak / Azure AD / Cognito; relevant once you expose endpoints to BI tools with their own SSO.

entries.title: A ClickHouse 25.8 Detective Story: High Memory Usage
entries.body: system.metric\_log now has 1,500+ columns; wide-part merges hold every column stream in memory and OOM-kill idle clusters. Fix: raise min\_bytes\_for\_wide\_part before production traffic.

entries.title: KB — Handy queries for system.query\_log
entries.body: Cluster-wide slow-query analysis SQL grouped by normalized query hash, with a CPU / disk / network / ZK-wait breakdown — the foundation for your Grafana dashboards.

entries.title: KB — When the SYSTEM database gets out of hand
entries.body: \_log tables grow unbounded; ship a z\_log\_disable.xml but keep query\_log + part\_log with TTL. Setting TTL matters more than disabling.

entries.title: KB — ClickHouse Monitoring (collated)
entries.body: Every maintained exporter plus Altinity's Grafana dashboards and Prometheus alert rules in the operator repo — a vetted starter alert set even off Kubernetes.

entries.title: Understanding Detached Parts in ClickHouse
entries.body: What detached parts mean, why they appear, and how to reattach or clean them.

entries.title: ClickHouse MVs and the one-primary-index workaround
entries.body: ClickHouse's one-primary-index-per-table constraint, and serving a second sort order with a re-sorted MV or projection.

entries.title: ClickHouse Mutations — what UPDATE/DELETE really cost
entries.body: Mutations rewrite parts in the background, and UPDATE is rejected on ORDER BY / partition columns — the cost model to understand before you ALTER.

entries.title: Lakehouses: a path to low-cost, no-lock-in observability
entries.body: Iceberg/Delta for observability at scale — with the explicit note that Iceberg has no sparse-primary or inverted index like ClickHouse uses for granular pruning.

entries.title: KFC: Kafka, Flink & ClickHouse blueprint (Mux)
entries.body: How Mux replaced an entire Flink layer with cascading MVs + Null tables at \~500K writes/sec with sub-minute lag — and when that's the right call.

entries.title: Real-time aggregations with ClickHouse MVs (80% cost cut)
entries.body: Migrating real-time event aggregation off Postgres to ClickHouse MVs for an 80% operational-cost cut — the pattern and the numbers.

entries.title: MV rebuild infrastructure (GitLab issue)
entries.body: GitLab's fix for MVs drifting from source: build a tmp\_ MV, backfill it, then EXCHANGE TABLES to atomic-swap it into place.

entries.title: chschema — schema-as-code (PostHog)
entries.body: PostHog's schema-as-code tool for managing ClickHouse DDL in version control.

entries.title: From OLTP to OLAP: 7 ClickHouse® Optimization Mistakes
entries.body: Seven rules from real customer tuning: filter before the join, sort key matches the filters (upper(country) defeats it, so normalize at ingest), LowCardinality for repeated strings, MV joins only fire on the left table, few large partitions. Measured result: endpoint p95 CPU from \~5s to under 1s, workload moved to one third the capacity. The MV join trigger rule is the one to repeat to the team.

entries.title: Self-hosted vs managed ClickHouse
entries.body: Vendor framed but the self hosted half is a good runbook: 3 node Keeper never on the database boxes; add a replica to remote_servers only once queue_size and absolute_delay are zero; recent defaults delay inserts at 1000 parts per partition and throw at 3000; SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA when the queue drifts from Keeper. Tinybird's first prod upgrade took 3h after 2 weeks of prep. Directly applicable to any self-hosted cluster.

entries.title: Lightweight deletes for Tinybird Data Sources now in Beta
entries.body: Lightweight DELETE writes a hidden _row_exists mask instead of rewriting parts; reads filter it at once, physical removal waits for merges. Can be scoped by partition. Note: ClickHouse does not report affected rows, so counts are computed beforehand. Relevant for GDPR style deletes on CDC fed tables versus ALTER TABLE … DELETE mutations.

entries.title: Cluster Management: keep the controls, skip the cluster ops
entries.meta: Tinybird · Aitana Azcona, Sep 2026, product post
entries.body: Product launch, but the resize pattern transfers: add new replicas, wait, shift weighted round robin read / write traffic, verify latency and queues, then remove old replicas; pay for overlap. Concurrency guard via old_weights. A clean template for a no downtime vertical resize on a self-managed cluster.

entries.title: From 48 Seconds to 130 Milliseconds: Vector Search in Tinybird
entries.meta: Tinybird · Daniel Sangorrín, May 2026, post (missed earlier)
entries.body: 19.35M × 768d embeddings. Each data part holds its own HNSW graph, so monthly partitions gave 58 graphs and 15–48s queries; one partition + OPTIMIZE FINAL gave one graph. Then the \~35GB index overflowed the 5GB default vector_similarity_index_cache_size; at 40GB queries fell to \~26ms, and stayed \~80–200ms for LIMIT 1,000. Part 2 (continuous ingest) not yet published. Relevant to semantic search in DENG-2357.

entries.title: Finding and fixing bugs in ClickHouse®'s Alias table engine
entries.meta: Tinybird · Enric Calabuig, Apr 2026, post (missed earlier)
entries.body: The experimental Alias engine forwards reads and writes to a target table (useful for zero downtime routing during migrations). Two bugs: unqualified targets were resolved against the session database, breaking check_referential_table_dependencies (fixed, PR #95175); inserts through an Alias did not trigger MVs on the target (fixed upstream in PR #94890). Check your version before using Alias as a swap layer.

entries.title: Important Security Advisory for Altinity Builds of ClickHouse®
entries.body: Three issues: a Brotli decoder crash on crafted requests (all versions since 19.3.3), a compromised CA in base Debian images, and CVE-2026-116366, an unauthenticated remote code execution for anyone with network access (details embargoed until 13 Nov; fix still in progress at posting). Patched upstream images exist on DockerHub but were not yet formally released: 26.3.62.3, 26.8.36.3, 26.9.27.3, 26.10.3.7. If you run Altinity builds, check your version and who can reach ports 8123 / 9000.

entries.title: Common Mistakes when Designing Schema for Log Data in ClickHouse®
entries.meta: Altinity · Dmitry Titov, Oct 2026, deep dive
entries.body: On ClickHouse's own TextBench OTel logs (1B rows): 39.5 GiB → 16.8 GiB and 16% faster queries. A Map column with \~2,000 distinct values went 16.1 GiB → 60 MiB as LowCardinality(String); drop ZSTD on small columns, ZSTD(3) on heavy ones; optimize_row_order only applies to new inserts, so OPTIMIZE FINAL won't do it, re-insert; skip index materialization on insert and force compact level 0 parts. Strong checklist for any event table.

entries.title: Introducing CAS: Drop-in Compute-Storage Separation for ClickHouse® MergeTree Tables
entries.body: Open source answer to SharedMergeTree in the Antalya 26.6 build: each part file stored once in S3 under its content hash, immutable manifests, coordination state in the bucket, GC by reachability (proved in TLA+). Fixes the orphan object problem that got zero copy deprecated upstream. Experimental; fine for cold tier, inserts not yet performant; S3 and GCS only. A new replica came up in 14s with no data copy.

entries.title: Is It Safe? Letting AI Agents Touch Production Data without the Tears
entries.body: Opens with an agent that set max_table_size_to_drop to 0 and then dropped a prod table. Guardrails belong in the database: a read only role, a settings profile (readonly, max threads, execution time), a quota, row policies, OAuth short lived tokens, an MCP server that never hands the LLM a DB credential, and no kubectl / cloud CLIs in the agent's sandbox. A direct checklist before giving any agent database access.

entries.title: Essential Tips for Safely Upgrading to Altinity Stable® 26.3
entries.body: Upgrade 25.8 → 26.3 is safe; downgrade is not unless you prepare. Pre-checks for removed features (Object type, hypothesis indexes, LIVE VIEW, QPL/QAT codecs) and pending mutations / DDL queue. Set 25.8 in the default profile before the first start to keep new parts readable by 25.8. Note async_insert now defaults to 1. Rebuild text indexes afterwards. Go one LTS at a time.

entries.title: ClickHouse® Keeper: The Long Road from "ZooKeeper in C++" to Something More
entries.meta: Altinity · Mikhail Filimonov, Aug 2026, deep dive
entries.body: Why Keeper used to lose to ZooKeeper (one session's read flushed every session's write batch; underfilled pipeline; NuRaft followers blocked on fsync, so writes cost 3–4 fsyncs instead of 1–2) and how 26.6 (PR #101757) made it \~2× faster: matches ZooKeeper on latency, beats it on throughput. Also the ZooKeeper zxid rollover failure mode. If an old benchmark kept you on ZooKeeper, rerun it on 26.6.

entries.title: ClickHouse Observability at Scale: 7 Costly Schema Mistakes We Measured
entries.body: 20M synthetic OTel logs on 26.9.2.8. A service, severity, time sort key read 1 of 2,442 granules for the top dashboard query; promoting map keys and Body fields to MATERIALIZED columns with bloom / set indexes cut reads 25 to 1,265× for +14% storage; 2,400 single row inserts made 2,400 parts, and async inserts cut that 12× but slowed each client 4×; a pod and status MV wrote 1.75M rows per 2.4M input; adding pod name to a rollup took reduction from 113.8× to 1.4×. Also an attribute census query and coalesce normalization for OTel semconv drift (http.status_code vs http.response.status_code). Pairs with the Altinity log schema post.

entries.title: Apache Kafka performance #1 — linger.ms
entries.body: Kafka 4.0 changed the producer default linger.ms from 0 to 5. What matters is the per producer, per partition send rate, not cluster throughput: expected batch ≈ 1 + linger\_seconds × rate. At 5K rec/s across 120 producers, linger 5 only added latency; on a 100K rec/s keyed workload, linger 20 took p99.9 from 700+ ms to 23 ms. Check batch sizes on the Debezium / producer side before tuning Flink.

entries.title: Kafka Share Groups and Parallelizing Consumption (series)

Includes the broker visible vs client local parallelism side post. Relevant if you need queue semantics on Kafka.

entries.body: MySQL → Iceberg hands-on. Crucial production detail buried in the tutorial: checkpointing is disabled by default and must be enabled to commit Iceberg transactions; the mysql-cdc binlog phase requires a complete checkpoint to avoid binlog disorder.

entries.body: The canonical talk. Wu designed the Flink-Iceberg integration. Compares Kafka vs Iceberg as streaming sources and walks the stream-processing use cases the Iceberg source can power. 48 minutes. Watch this before anything else in this section.

entries.title: Apple Meetup — Streaming from Iceberg Data Lake & Multi Cluster Kafka Source
entries.meta: Wu et al. · Apple, Jun 2022, talk
entries.body: Companion talk plus the multi-cluster Kafka source — directly relevant to multi-cluster Kafka setups.

entries.title: Iceberg Flink Queries & Streaming Read (official docs)
entries.body: The API surface. OPTIONS('streaming'='true', 'monitor-interval'='1s') in SQL hints; start-snapshot-id to start from a specific point. FLIP-27 source toggle via table.exec.iceberg.use-flip27-source = true is the gotcha — most blog code uses the old SourceFunction interface.

entries.title: Announcing Fluss 0.7
entries.body: Lake tiering service made stateless and pluggable across Iceberg/Paimon. The pivot away from "lake tier is a Flink job with sync offsets in Flink State" — single point of failure, opaque state. Sync offset now lives in Fluss metadata.

entries.title: Apache Fluss vs Apache Paimon — Two engines for the real-time lakehouse
entries.body: The Taobao case is the eye-opener: Fluss replaces dual-stream joins with Delta Joins — querying Fluss directly instead of caching the dimension table in Flink state — and cut a 100 TB job's checkpoint from 90 s to 1 s.

entries.title: When Paimon Beats Iceberg for Mutable Streams
entries.body: When to pick Paimon vs Iceberg. Paimon: high-frequency CDC, Flink-native execution, real-time freshness required, steeper LSM-tuning curve. Iceberg: larger user base, more documented failure patterns, better catalog tooling. Read before committing either way.

entries.title: Fluss Streaming Lakehouse Quickstart
entries.body: The actual wiring. Flink reads the latest Paimon snapshot via the tiering service, then switches to Fluss from the aligned log offset — exactly-once semantics across the boundary. The union-read pattern that makes warm/cold work.

sections.name: The Tableflow paradigm — Kafka segments as Iceberg

entries.title: Introducing Tableflow — Unifying streaming & analytics
entries.body: The Kora Storage Layer takes Kafka segments and writes them out as parquet. Materialize topics as Iceberg or Delta Lake tables in a click. The architectural pivot: you don't ingest into a lakehouse anymore; the streaming layer is the lakehouse.

entries.title: Tableflow Docs (Confluent Cloud)
entries.body: Automatic schematization, type conversions, schema evolution, CDC stream materialization, catalog publishing. Tables read by any analytics engine without duplication. Flink sits before Tableflow if you need transformations — not between Kafka and the lake.

entries.title: Kafka to Iceberg — Exploring the options
entries.body: The honest comparison piece. Walks every option side-by-side: Flink SQL, Kafka Connect Iceberg sink, Tableflow, multi-cluster-to-single-table. Moffat is the most reliable independent voice in the Kafka world. Read before deciding the path.

entries.title: Sending Data to Apache Iceberg from Apache Kafka with Apache Flink
entries.meta: Robin Moffat · Decodable, Jul 2024, open-source path
entries.body: Open-source hands-on counterpart to Tableflow. MinIO for storage, Hive Metastore catalog, Flink SQL for both the ingest and inline transformations.

entries.title: From Stream to Lakehouse — Kafka ingestion with the Flink Dynamic Iceberg Sink
entries.body: The most current production pattern. Dynamic sink writes to multiple Iceberg tables with full schema evolution. A single unified pipeline ingests from any number of topics, writes to any number of tables, handles new topics and schema changes without restarts.

entries.title: Questioning the Lambda Architecture
entries.meta: Jay Kreps · O'Reilly Radar, 2014, the original
entries.body: The original. The piece that named Kappa and argued Lambda's dual-code burden was avoidable if you treat the log as primary and replay through a single stream processor. Worth re-reading every few years; everything since is a footnote.

entries.title: The Rise of Kappa Architecture in the Era of Agentic AI and Data Streaming
entries.body: Current state-of-play. Open table formats and Shift-Left principles position Kappa as the foundation for governed data platforms. Confluent-leaning voice but well-sourced and current.

entries.title: From Kappa Architecture to Streamhouse — Making the Lakehouse real-time
entries.body: The architectural evolution. Streamhouse combines real-time streaming with Lakehouse analytics, driven by Paimon and Fluss integrated with Flink. The architectural bet behind Grab's Hugo and the CDP scenarios you already know.

entries.title: Introduction to Unified Batch & Stream Processing of Apache Flink
entries.body: The Flink-native framing — and the honest "Kappa isn't free either" piece. Kappa removes the batch layer and gets replay from message-queue retention, but cannot provide batch benefits; backtracking performance is inferior to batch.

entries.title: The Kappa Architecture — Simplifying data pipelines with streaming
entries.body: Practical decision lens. Kappa works when processing logic is the same for real-time and historical. Lambda forces dual codebases (Spark for batch, Flink for streaming). Read for the decision framework, not the architecture history.

sections.name: Backfilling in Kappa — the hardest problem

entries.title: Designing a Production-Ready Kappa Architecture for Timely Data Stream Processing
entries.body: The seminal article on Kappa backfill. Both common methodologies — replaying Hive into Kafka, and backfilling as a batch job — failed to scale. Solution: model the Hive connector as a streaming source. Spark Streaming implementation but principles apply to Flink. The mistake-list alone is worth the read.

entries.title: Backfill Streaming Data Pipelines in Kappa Architecture
entries.meta: Waibel & Ananthanarayanan · Netflix, Data + AI Summit deck
entries.body: The Flink-native counterpart to Uber's piece. RMI (Real-time Merched Impression) joins Impression with Playback events for play attribution — one of the largest stateful Flink apps at Netflix. Backfill in Kappa style using the Data Lake plus the event-ordering challenges they hit.

entries.title: Unified Flink Source at Pinterest — Streaming data processing
entries.body: Kafka retention is 3 days to under 8 hours; replaying historical via Kafka costs 20× the infrastructure. Solution: Merced stores data on S3 keeping original event ordering and partitions; UnifiedSource combines FlinkKafkaConsumer and MercedFileSource per SubTask. Same architectural shape as Grab's Hugo.

entries.title: Engineering a Reliable Data Backfill Solution
entries.body: The operational hack you need. 600 MB/s scale with stateful Flink for sessionization. Backfill line: backups + tooling + dedicated Kafka cluster + sandbox replica of prod.

entries.title: Parallelizing Historic Backfills with Flink
entries.body: The implementation deep-dive. Hits the watermark-divergence problem directly: parallelizing across key groups means fast threads race ahead and slow threads' valid records arrive "late," getting dropped from windows. Fix: Java CyclicBarrier for lockstep progress.

entries.title: Dynamic CDC with Flink CDC and Consistent Hashing
entries.meta: Goldsky, Flink Forward 2023, CDC war story
entries.body: CDC backfill war story. "Things didn't work — the connector tried to use the replication slot during snapshotting." The algorithm that fixed it: stop live event processing → read next chunk → resume live → reconcile via watermarks.

entries.title: Flink CDC Incremental Snapshot Framework
entries.body: The modern auto-managed backfill. Distributed chunk-based scanning; checkpoint at chunk level resolves the timeout problem of the old snapshot mechanism; no global read lock. Gotcha: non-uniform PK distribution leads to unbalanced tasks during snapshot read.

entries.title: Principle Analysis of Apache Flink CDC Batch & Stream Integration
entries.body: The algorithm explainer. Binlog read from an offset, snapshot split for a key found, its max binlog offset found; current offset > max → send, else discard. MySqlHybridSplitAssigner, MySqlValidator. Read after the docs if you want the why.

entries.title: Backfill Upsert Table via Flink/Pinot Connector
entries.meta: Yupeng Fu · Uber, RTA Summit 2023, specialty path
entries.body: The upsert-target backfill workaround. Generate upsert segments directly from batch sources like Hive — no Kafka dependency. The pattern generalizes to any "must be real-time" sink (Pinot, some StarRocks setups, some ClickHouse configurations).

entries.title: How Uber Manages Petabytes of Real-Time Data
entries.body: "Kappa+" is Uber's coinage — the canonical name for "Kappa with first-class backfill." Active-Active Kafka, FlinkSQL, Pinot upserts. Higher-level summary connecting the pieces.

entries.title: How Uber uses Apache Kafka in production
entries.body: Kafka tiered storage via KIP-405 changes the Kappa-backfill calculus by extending Kafka retention cheaply. Recent log segments on broker disk, older offloaded transparently to HDFS/S3/GCS/Azure. May reduce the need for a Merced-style sidecar entirely.

entries.title: Backfilling historical data with pipelines
entries.body: Cleanest conceptual reference. Scenarios needing backfill, considerations (idempotency, schema compatibility, SLA-sized batches). Databricks-specific implementation (ONCE flow), generic principles that transfer.

entries.title: Flink Kubernetes Operator 1.14.0
entries.body: Native Blue/Green deployment support for stateful streaming applications. People have been hand-rolling this pattern for years — now upstream.

entries.title: Flink Kubernetes Operator — Autoscaler
entries.meta: Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator, official docs
entries.body: Works best with Kafka sources (standardized connector metrics). Auto-detects source max parallelism from Kafka partition count. Requires the new Source API exposing the busyTime metric. Context: this is upstream — Grab's Predictive Resource Advisor sits on top of, not instead of.

entries.title: Get Running with Apache Flink on Kubernetes (Parts 1 & 2)
entries.body: Vendor-authored but unbiased Operator walkthrough. Installation, custom resources, fault tolerance, HA, savepoints, observability, UI access. Good first-touch reference.

entries.title: Apache Flink 2.3.0 Release Announcement
entries.meta: Flink PMC, Jun 2026, release (from the announcement and release PR, not read in full)
entries.body: Changelog conversion operators in SQL (moving between upsert and append streams in SQL rather than Java), more flexible materialized tables, the experimental native S3 filesystem (next entry), application management and rescale history for elastic scaling, plus a BITMAP type and NDU analyzer improvements. 2.3 is now the stable docs line, with 1.20 as LTS. The changelog operators matter most for SQL-first teams.

entries.title: Introducing Flink's Native S3 FileSystem: Built for Performance, Designed for Production
entries.meta: Flink PMC · Gabor Somogyi & Samrat Deb, Jun 2026, post
entries.body: flink-s3-fs-native: Hadoop free, on AWS SDK v2, one plugin for both FileSystem and RecoverableWriter (so exactly once FileSink, which Presto lacked). Benchmark vs the Presto plugin: \~2.17× throughput, average checkpoint 48.8s vs 90.1s, P99 76.7s vs 165.3s. Mostly a drop in jar swap; one way migration (Hadoop / Presto sink state restores on native, not the reverse). Worth testing for checkpoints and Iceberg writes on object storage.

entries.title: Apache Flink CDC 3.7.0 Release Announcement
entries.meta: Flink PMC · Xiqian Yu, Oct 2026, release
entries.body: Notable reliability fixes: MySQL CDC sources stuck during binlog backfill (FLINK-39621, FLINK-39315), newly added table recovery after region failover, the Iceberg sink writing duplicates when a schema change splits writes in a checkpoint or an update moves partitions (FLINK-38450/40640), and Debezium JSON with column defaults. Also new: an existing table schema CHECK / EXPAND mode for sinks, a SQL Server source, and AI transform functions in YAML pipelines.

entries.title: Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator 1.16.0 Release Announcement
entries.meta: Flink PMC · Dennis-Mircea Ciupitu, Sep 2026, release (not read; linked from the Flink homepage)
entries.body: Focused on extensibility and a restructured documentation set; follows 1.14's native Blue/Green deployments (indexed above).

entries.title: Apache Flink Agents 0.4.0 Release Announcement
entries.meta: Flink PMC · Wenjin Xie, Oct 2026, release (not read in full)
entries.body: AI agents inside Flink streaming pipelines, with Flink's distributed execution and fault recovery. Still a preview, but billed as the last step before 1.0; 0.3 (Jun) added a YAML API, Mem0 long term memory and a Fluss backed action state store. Watch, don't adopt yet; it could eventually host event-driven agents next to existing pipelines.

entries.title: Materialized Tables in Apache Flink
entries.meta: Robin Moffatt (rmoff.net, mirrored on dev.to), Apr 2026, hands-on
entries.body: FLIP-435 materialized tables (since 1.20) put the populate-and-refresh SQL inside the table definition, compared with CREATE TABLE + INSERT and CTAS. They need a catalog that supports them plus a scheduler (the SQL Gateway ships a basic one); only Paimon and the test-filesystem catalog support everything. Gotcha: Iceberg's Flink catalog does not support them. Robin's Iceberg PR #16079 replaces the cryptic error with a clear one. Check this before planning on 2.3's materialized table features on an Iceberg catalog such as Polaris.

entries.title: Alternatives to MinIO for single-node local S3
entries.body: MinIO was abandoned as an open project in late 2025, so he swapped seven alternatives into a DuckDB + Iceberg REST Docker Compose stack: • S3Proxy was the easiest drop-in; SeaweedFS and Zenko CloudServer were also easy. • RustFS is still alpha and recently had a serious vulnerability. • Garage needs real config (newer versions add a single-node flag), Ozone wouldn't run on fewer than four nodes, and Ceph is too heavy. Later update: the pgsty/minio fork promises CVE patches. Compose files are in rmoff/minio-alternatives. Relevant to local dev and CI stacks.

entries.title: Claude Code isn't going to replace data engineers (yet)
entries.meta: Robin Moffatt, Mar 2026, eval (not read in full)
entries.body: He had Claude Code build an idiomatic dbt + DuckDB project (staging → dim/fact) against his earlier hand-built pipeline. The answer was "good, but not a replacement, yet." Companion post: Evaluating Claude's dbt Skills: Building an Eval from Scratch (13 Mar). A useful method for testing your own agent workflows.

entries.meta: Robin Moffatt, Sep 2026, newsletter (Kafka / Flink heavy edition)
entries.body: Leads for the next refresh: • Lorenzo Nicora's two-part watermarks deep dive. • Gustavo de Morais on custom CDC with FROM_CHANGELOG / TO_CHANGELOG, the Flink 2.3 changelog operators. • David Anderson on deduplicating streams and reviewing Flink SQL. • Why Lyft moved to the Flink Kubernetes Operator. • Tyler Akidau et al., The Dataflow Model Revisited. • DuckDB Labs joining AWS, with projects staying open source.

name: Agentic Data
blurb: Data agents, context layers and streaming agents on Flink. The theme across every serious write-up: the model is not the hard part; curated, owned, governed context is.

entries.title: How we built a personal data scientist for every Notion employee
entries.body: Weekly requests to the data team fell about 80% in two months; about half of employees use it. Three pillars: governed access (every user signs in to Snowflake with their own identity, so answers reflect their grants), shared context (a Notion database indexing Skills, Metric Definitions, Table Schemas and FAQs, read page by page, not loaded whole) and clear instructions (resolve metric, population, period first; check join cardinality, denominators, incomplete periods; flag missing definitions instead of improvising). A run_tagged_query wrapper stamps each SQL with metric, definition and question metadata for tracing. Nightly review agent scans conversations, Slack, Notion and GitHub for stale or conflicting context; a triage agent applies small fixes and escalates the rest ("evidence isn't approval"). Spinoffs: Data Scout Reporter for scheduled reports, domain agents reusing its MCP. Takeaway: per-user identity, a definitions index, query tagging and a review loop.

entries.title: How to build a data agent in Notion (help guide)
entries.body: The companion how-to: connection choices, example instructions, routing guidance, maintenance workflows and query logging examples. Notes that the wrapper is their internal implementation; the reusable parts are standard instructions, structured logging and metadata added at execution. Good source of instruction templates.

entries.title: Inside OpenAI's in-house data agent
entries.meta: OpenAI · Bonnie Xu, Aravind Suresh, Emma Tang, Jan 2026, architecture
entries.body: Over 70k datasets and 600 PB for 3.5k+ internal users, reachable from Slack, web, IDEs and MCP. Built on multiple layers of context (table usage metadata, human annotations, code level enrichment that reads the pipelines producing each table, institutional knowledge, memory, live queries). Memory alone took one test question from 22 minutes to about 1.5 minutes. The "code enrichment" idea maps well to reading Flink SQL and ClickHouse MV definitions to explain what a table really contains.

entries.title: How OpenAI Built Its Data Agent
entries.meta: ByteByteGo · interview with Emma Tang, 2026, interview
entries.body: Why the agent is deliberately "pretty vanilla": one LLM, a context assembly layer, a curated tool set and a runtime. Strong data foundations do the work, not agent complexity. Good counterweight to over-engineering a data agent.

entries.title: Introducing Genie One, Genie Agents, and Genie Ontology
entries.body: Genie Ontology automatically extracts knowledge from tables, queries, dashboards, pipelines and connected apps into a living graph, then weights each definition PageRank style by source, author authority, how often people rely on it, links to certified assets, and freshness, answering from the highest weighted sources and only from content the user may see. Self reported: 84.5% first attempt accuracy on a 28 question suite vs 52.4% for the strongest coding agent. Genie One also lives in Teams and Slack. The ranking idea is worth copying cheaply, e.g. prefer verified questions and curated segments over ad hoc tables.

entries.title: Pushing the Frontier for Data Agents with Genie
entries.body: Three techniques behind the accuracy jump: specialized knowledge search over a semantic index of tables, notebooks and dashboards; multiple LLMs with prompts tuned via GEPA; and parallel thinking. Reported internal accuracy rose from 32% (coding agent baseline) to over 90%.

entries.title: Databricks Genie Ontology and the Semantic Layer Consolidation
entries.body: Sober take: Genie Ontology is a context layer, not a semantic layer; it is in gated preview; and context accuracy is not answer accuracy. The benchmark is 28 self graded questions. Read before quoting vendor numbers to leadership.

entries.title: NVIDIA Auto Ontology
entries.body: An open library that builds the agent context layer from enterprise metadata: Discover (generate an ontology, link existing semantic models), Ground (attach trusted business meaning, reconcile definitions across systems), Expose (serve it to any agent via MCP, CLI or API), Learn (fold certified corrections back in). Stored in Postgres. The most directly reusable artifact on this list; check connector coverage for your stack before investing.

entries.title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
entries.body: Walkthrough of the tools (e.g. a readiness check before querying), a comparison table against other semantic layers (listed sources: Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, DuckDB), NVIDIA's claim of 90% faster ontology build, and the NeMo Gym evaluation comparing schema only vs ontology grounded agents.

entries.title: NVIDIA Adds a Knowledge Layer to Its Agent Toolkit
entries.body: Context for Auto Ontology: NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation, Kumo relational models, NVIDIA's own supply chain agents running through Palantir Foundry Ontology, and Databricks pairing Kumo Anomaly with Genie Ontology. The "ontology" vocabulary in one place.

entries.title: DoorDash Gives 10,000 Employees an AI Data Analyst (Vera)
entries.meta: PYMNTS coverage of DoorDash Engineering's "Inside Vera" post, Oct 2026, news (original post not opened)
entries.body: Pass rate on their 1,900 question eval rose from 43% to 90%, and they credit data organization over model choice. Same model head to head: Vera 73% vs an off the shelf coding agent 48%, which struggled to pick tables. Vera is blocked from unverified data; analysts now own the semantic layer and the eval set. Lesson: build a fixed eval set of real questions before adding features.

entries.title: What Is a Context Layer for AI Agents? The Definitive Guide for 2026
entries.body: Ties together OpenAI's six layers, Snowflake's agent context layer and a16z's "superset of the semantic layer": a context layer adds entity resolution, policy and governance enforcement at the agent boundary, and memory of past decisions. MCP is plumbing, not a substitute for governed context.

entries.title: FLIP-531: Initiate Flink Agents as a new Sub-Project
entries.meta: Xintong Song, Sean Falconer, Chris Meyers · Flink wiki, May 2025, design doc
entries.body: The founding proposal: minimal runtime infrastructure for long running, event driven agents built on existing Flink primitives, with Table and DataStream APIs as input and output.

entries.title: Event-Driven AI Agents: Why Flink Agents Are the Future of Enterprise AI
entries.body: Agents as event driven microservices: one runtime for data and agents, checkpointing for consistency across transformations and agent decisions, native MCP tool calls, dynamic topologies for ReAct style loops, and observability of decisions.

entries.title: Alibaba Cloud, Ververica, Confluent, and LinkedIn Join Forces on Streaming AI Agents
entries.body: The Flink Forward Barcelona 2025 announcement; links Alibaba's deep dive and the Flink Forward Asia talk.

entries.title: Apache Flink Agents 0.3.0 Release Announcement

entries.body: Mem0 backed long term memory, a declarative YAML API for agents in Python and Java, cross language actions, Fluss as action state store alongside Kafka, EventLog in the Web UI.

entries.title: Orchestrating Autonomous AI Agents with Apache Kafka and Apache Flink
entries.meta: Sandon Jacobs (Confluent) · All Things Open 2026, slides + demo
entries.body: Clearest mental model: a Flink agent is an event loop, not a call stack; LLMs as stateful operators in the DAG; durable memory survives restarts. Demo code linked from the deck. Start here for hands on.

entries.title: Event-driven Agents with Complex Event Processing in Flink
entries.body: Calling an LLM per event is costly and non deterministic, so filter first with Flink CEP and anomaly detection, then let a small model classify or act on the detected patterns. Exactly the shape for anomaly alerts on Kafka streams.
